title: Dry-run: direct upload and async transcoding

spec.title: Dry-run: direct upload and async transcoding
spec.intro: About 5 minutes. The app server never touches file bytes — that single decision shapes everything else here.

steps.title: Never proxy the bytes through your API
steps.explain: Routing a video upload through the app server ties up a request thread for the whole transfer and burns bandwidth you're paying for twice. The API's only job is to issue a short-lived signed URL; the client uploads straight to object storage.
steps.saysOutLoud: The app server issues a permission slip, it never sees the file itself.

steps.title: Large files upload in parts, not one PUT
steps.explain: A single-request upload dies on any network blip and restarts from zero. Multipart upload splits the file into chunks the client can retry independently, and only the failed chunk needs resending.

steps.title: Storage fires an event; the app never polls
steps.explain: Object storage emits an event on object-created directly to a queue. The app doesn't poll storage asking 'is it done yet' — it reacts to the event, which also means the upload can succeed even if the app server is temporarily down.

steps.title: The transcode job is a fan-out to multiple renditions
steps.explain: One upload becomes several outputs — a few resolutions, maybe a thumbnail — because different clients and network conditions need different bitrates. Each rendition is its own job so one failing (say, 4K on a slow encoder) doesn't block the others from going live.

steps.title: Transcoding itself runs outside the app entirely
steps.explain: Actual encoding (ffmpeg or a managed service like MediaConvert) is CPU-bound and can take minutes — nothing an API request should ever wait on. Workers pull transcode jobs from the queue, write each output back to storage under a predictable key, and mark that rendition ready independently.

steps.title: Serve only what's marked ready
steps.explain: The player has to handle 'video exists but 1080p isn't done yet' as a normal state, not an error — falling back to whatever rendition is currently available rather than erroring out or blocking on the highest quality.

spec.closing: If they ask about failed uploads: the presigned URL expires and the pending row never flips to complete, so a cleanup job sweeping 'pending for over 24h' is enough — no special-case error handling needed on the happy path.
